newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Rwandan jails, courts worry U.N. Security Council.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan jails, courts worry U.N. Security Council.

text.p: Security Council members are concerned about Rwanda's deteriorating prison conditions and poor judicial system and call on the government to improve them, council president Park Soo Gil said on Wednesday.
The South Korean diplomat was speaking to reporters after the council was briefed by Ibrahima Fall, assistant secretary-general for political affairs, on the situations in Rwanda and Burundi.

"Members of the council ... expressed concern over the continuing deterioration of prison conditions, lack of proper legal protection and the poor judicial system and called upon the Rwandan government to improve the situation in this regard," Park said.

They also expressed concern over the deterioration of the overall security situation in Rwanda and condemned attacks on the civilian population, particularly the killing of 17 schoolgirls on April 28 by Interahamwe militiamen.
Some Hutu militiamen who massacred Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 returned late in 1996 from Zaire and Tanzania with refugees who fled after the killings.
Many alleged perpetrators of the massacres were among thousands of prisoners in Rwanda's crammed jails.
Park said Security Council members also stressed that the Rwandan government must cooperate closely with the international tribunal set up to prosecute those responsible for the genocide.
On Burundi, he said concerns were expressed over "acts of violence by the combatants against the civilians and also the policy of forced resettlement by the Burundian government."

They took positive note of the political dialogue being conducted between the Burundi government and the armed opposition and said they appreciated the continuing efforts of regional leaders, in particular former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere, who is acting as a conciliator.

Burundi's military ruler, Pierre Buyoya, who took power in an army coup last July, said on Tuesday his government had made progress toward a ceasefire during direct talks in Rome with the main Hutu rebel group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
